transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Carlos (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Jordan (CTO Asterion), Maya (SRE), Ben (ML Eng), Olga (Security)

Optional auto sections:
Summary: Deep dive into tail latency observed in Asterion's VPC-based inference workloads. Focus areas: p95/p99 spikes, cold-starts with KV cache warm-up, streaming vs non-streaming trade-offs, multi-hop network effects on tail, and quantization interactions. Agreed next steps and a pilot bench inside customer VPC.
Topics: p95/p99 measurement, KV "cold cache" behavior, streaming chunking, batching windows, on-prem/VPC network topology, KMS/HSM key rotation concerns.
Action items: see metadata list.

Transcript:
[00:00] Carlos: okay hey everyone thanks for taking the time, i'm Carlos from Redwood, with Priya and Liam on the SE side. how's everyone doing today?
[00:08] Jordan: good hey thanks, excited to dig in — we've been seeing these intermittent p99 blips and curious if it's the kv path or network microbursts.
[00:15] Priya: great, quick agenda — we'll reproduce your p95/p99 locally, walk topology, run a couple of controlled benches, and then discuss mitigation (streaming chunking, aggressive prefix caching, batching windows, maybe quantization). sound ok?
[00:28] Maya: yes that's the ask. we've got a VPC peering to Redwood's private control plane but data path stays in our VPC. we also sometimes route through an internal proxy cluster which could add hops.
[00:40] Ben: adding — most traffic is short prompts (avg 120 tokens), but we have a heavy tail of long-completion analytics flows 2-3% that go 2k+ tokens.
[00:50] Liam: that long tail is often the culprit for sequence length variance. we need to see how the runtime handles kv evictions + kv rehydration on those requests.
[01:02] Priya: quick clarifying q — when you say p99 blip, are we talking absolute latency jumps or tail of token stream (streaming stalls)?
[01:09] Jordan: both. sometimes the whole request is delayed (end-to-end), sometimes streaming stalls mid-response for 2-4s then resumes.
[01:18] Priya: ok noted. two hypotheses: 1) multi-hop network serialization (internal proxy + peering + edge), 2) KV cache cold path when a rare token/sequence misses causing re-computation or slow disk fetch depending on cache tier.
[01:32] Maya: yes our ops team mentioned occasional egress NAT port exhaustion, which could manifest as ephemeral connection stalls.
[01:40] Carlos: uh-huh, that would show as TCP retry stalls — visible in p99 but not in median. we should capture tcp retrans metrics.
[01:47] Ben: we can pull flow logs, but we wanted to understand best mitigations on the Redwood side before we commit infra changes.
[01:55] Priya: makes sense. I'll sketch the runtime flow — bear with me if the names get fuzzy, i always mix kv cache vs k v cash in my head, sorry —
[02:03] Priya: request enters edge proxy -> auth -> routing to dedicated serving pod -> request deserializes and checks prefix KV cache -> if hit, attach KV pointers and stream tokens; if miss, runtime triggers KV fetch from backing store (hot tier in memory, cold tier SSD or remote kv service) -> model execution resumes.
[02:25] Jordan: so the miss path can be multi-tier. what's the typical added latency for an SSD-backed kv miss?
[02:32] Priya: ballpark: memory hit ~200-600us, remote memstore ~1-3ms, SSD cold fetch can be 8-30ms depending on IO queueing; but rehydration and model warm-up can add ~50-200ms if kv sharding triggers other work.
[02:49] Maya: but we're seeing 2-4s pauses not 30ms — could that be connection stalls?
[02:55] Liam: yes, 2-4s often point to network retry or higher-level timeouts. also streaming stalls can happen if backpressure on the stream buffer occurs — e.g., downstream proxy momentarily refuses packets.
[03:08] Ben: our proxy cluster metrics show occasional GC pauses on the proxy hosts at ~3s, that's suspicious.
[03:14] Priya: that would align. two parallel mitigations: push stronger prefix caching to reduce misses, and implement streaming keepalive + smaller chunk sizes to make streaming resilient to microbursts.
[03:27] Jordan: can you explain smaller chunks? doesn't that hurt latency?
[03:31] Priya: tradeoff, yep. larger chunks reduce per-token overhead and are more efficient for throughput, but increase time-to-first-byte for later tokens if a chunk stalls. smaller chunks (e.g., 32 tokens vs 128 tokens) reduce tail stall time but may increase CPU and network overhead. it's a UI/latency vs cost trade.
[03:51] Maya: our SLA focuses on p95, but product wants p99 < 500ms for chat flows.
[03:58] Carlos: p99 < 500ms for chat with your long tail is tough but we can approach with combined measures: aggressive prefix warming for common prompts, streaming chunk size tune, and cross-region routing to avoid NAT bottlenecks.
[04:14] Ben: where does quantization play? we've started using 4-bit models to cut cost.
[04:19] Priya: good point — quantization reduces computation time per token but can increase memory pressure on KV (more aggressive cache usage) and sometimes increases variability due to kernel selection differences. we've seen scenarios where quantized kernels fall back to slower emulation paths on certain GPUs causing p99 spikes.
[04:37] Liam: runtime picks optimized kernels; if a model variant uses a kernel that isn't fully supported on the instance type, we can get a fallback which costs milliseconds to tens of ms depending. mixed-precision mismatches also cause extra memcpy.
[04:49] Jordan: so we should pin quantized variant to known-good instance types in our dedicated pool?
[04:54] Priya: exactly. Redwood dedicated allows routing by model + instance compatibility. pinning reduces the chance of unexpected kernel fallback.
[05:02] Olga: on the security side, we need to ensure KMS/HSM rotation and audit logs don't block traffic. are there any synchronous KMS calls in the request path?
[05:10] Carlos: only at model load or key rewrap, those are async for token-level ops. but if you have custom envelope decryption per-request it could add latency.
[05:18] Maya: we do per-tenant key unwraps for some sensitive flows, maybe that aligns with some spikes.
[05:24] Priya: if key unwrap happens in the hot path it could add 50-200ms depending on HSM latencies, and if HSM is rate-limited that could create queueing spikes. best practice is cache unwrapped keys in-memory in the serving pod for a TTL and rotate behind the scenes.
[05:42] Ben: let's go into measurement strategy — we want to be sure p99 is real and reproducible. what should we benchmark?
[05:48] Priya: two benches: 1) end-to-end within your VPC using real traffic shapes (including NAT/proxy) to capture network hops; 2) isolated runtime bench with synthetic clients inside the same subnet to remove network variance and isolate KV/runtime behavior.
[06:02] Liam: important: exercise the long-completion flows — run a 5k request suite with 2-3% of requests at 2k tokens to see tail. collect tcp traces, runtime logs, and kv-hit timelines.
[06:15] Jordan: can Redwood run the inside-VPC bench or we need to provide runners?
[06:19] Priya: we can run runners if you grant a temporary job user via our AGENT container, or you can run the script — either is fine. we prefer you run it once and share logs for compliance reasons.
[06:30] Carlos: we'll send the bench harness (small go binary + YAML) and a one‑line to kick off. Priya will provide the configs.
[06:36] Jordan: perfect. also, is there a way to visualize kv miss distribution across requests?
[06:40] Priya: yes — runtime emits per-request kv_hit_ratio and kv_fetch_latencies. in the console you'll see a scatter of kv-miss vs latency. we'll also export a CSV for your SREs.
[06:50] Maya: what about streaming vs non-streaming? for our UI chat we prefer streaming, but for long analytic completions we usually do non-streaming with chunked flushes.
[06:58] Liam: non-streaming can mask mid-response stalls because the user only sees final output, meaning the p99 is end-to-end only. streaming exposes internal token-level stalls. each mode has different tolerance: streaming requires resilient chunking and keepalive to survive microbursts; non-streaming benefits from larger batches and also is sensitive to total compute time.
[07:17] Ben: is there an intermediate mode? like commit partial outputs while still buffering?
[07:21] Priya: yes we call it progressive flush — buffer modestly (e.g., 128 tokens) but flush partial results to maintain responsiveness. it's a compromise.
[07:30] Jordan: earlier you mentioned prefix caching. how do we avoid heavy memory pressure if we cache many prefixes?
[07:36] Priya: prioritization. store hot prefixes (top X templates) in-memory across serving pods; less common prefixes can be cached in an LRU shared cache with TTL. Redwood Optimize can analyze your prompt corpus and recommend which prefixes to warm.
[07:49] Carlos: reminder — if you have many tenants, per-tenant caches can explode memory; use a shared keyed cache with admission policies based on frequency.
[07:58] Maya: our prompts are highly templated per product line, should be trainable.
[08:02] Priya: another mitigation: KV prefetch for predicted next-token contexts for long-running sessions — speculative prefetch reduces miss probability but increases bandwidth. it's a tunable trade.
[08:14] Jordan: let's talk about network hops: we peer in region A, we route through internal proxy, then to an edge NAT, then to Redwood pod — that's like 3-4 hops. how much tail does each hop add?
[08:27] Liam: each hop adds base latency (1-3ms) but tail is multiplicative when you hit queueing or GC. one flaky proxy with 99th percentile 50ms can dominate your p99. TCP retransmits also amplify.
[08:39] Ben: so do you recommend removing internal proxy from datapath?
[08:43] Priya: if it can be bypassed for inference traffic, yes. If not, tune proxy GC and connection pools — ensure keepalives and sufficient ephemeral ports.
[08:53] Maya: earlier we mentioned NAT port exhaustion — mitigation there?
[08:57] Carlos: allocate larger NAT pools, use multiple egress gateways, or use VPC providers that support richer connection tracking. Redwood can also support static egress IPs from dedicated capacity to reduce translation churn.
[09:10] Jordan: good. are there telemetry flags we should enable to correlate p99 spikes across layers?
[09:15] Priya: enable per-request trace IDs, tcp-level metrics, kv_hit/latency, kernel fallback flags (runtime emits when kernel fallback occurs), and exporter of model-variant decisions. with these you can join traces.
[09:29] Olga: on compliance we need logs sanitized — can we sample traces or anonymize tokens?
[09:34] Carlos: yes Redwood supports token redaction in traces and sampled spans for diagnostics, and full audit logs for security teams if requested under NDA.
[09:43] Ben: quick detour — cold starts: do we see cold starts on dedicated pools?
[09:48] Priya: cold starts typically appear when autoscale spins up new GPU instances. Model load is the main cost (weight transfer to GPU, KV mapping, kernel JIT). typical coldstart 2-7s depending on model size; but with pre-warmed GPUs or pinned models coldstart ~200-800ms.
[10:05] Liam: we also have continuous keepalive lanes for async warm containers to reduce cold starts. it's a small cost but helps p99.
[10:13] Jordan: what's the recommendation for dedicated vs hosted here? we prefer dedicated for predictability.
[10:18] Carlos: Dedicated gives you pinned capacity and faster coldstart behavior because models can be burst-loaded and kept resident. Hosted is cheaper for spiky, but you pay for variability. Given your SLA, Dedicated with reserved warm containers + VPC private path is recommended.
[10:32] Maya: how about on-prem? Some teams want air-gapped on-prem for GDPR.
[10:36] Priya: on-prem adds more control but you inherit network topology issues. Redwood private can run on your infra with the same runtime; you'd still need to manage egress and KMS locally. tail issues push back to you for network configs.
[10:49] Ben: ok, let's go hands-on: Priya, can you show a quick log snippet of kv hit timeline?
[10:54] Priya: sure, i'll share screen — (screen share, some lag) —
[11:04] [screen-share noise] Priya: here, each row is a request; columns are request start, token1, kv-check, kv-fetch-time, kernel time, stream-chunk-send. see these rows where kv_fetch_time spikes and stream-chunk-send is delayed. sometimes kernel fallback flagged as "fallback_gemm".
[11:22] Jordan: interesting one at 11:10:23 shows kv_fetch 14ms but stream-chunk-send delayed 2.2s — that gap corresponds to a proxy GC at the same time.
[11:30] Maya: yep that's our GC window. we can tune the proxy but would like to reduce reliance.
[11:36] Priya: recommend steps: 1) run bench to reproduce; 2) pin quantized variant to known-good instance in dedicated pool; 3) enable prefix warm for top 50 templates; 4) reduce stream chunk size for chat flows to 32 tokens and enable progressive flush for analytics; 5) increase NAT port pool + remove proxy from hot path if possible.
[11:58] Jordan: sounds good. what about measuring improvement?
[12:01] Priya: compare p95/p99 histograms before/after, token-level stall counts, and kv_hit_ratio over time. we'll instrument bench to emit these.
[12:10] Carlos: i'll share a short runbook and the bench link after the call.
[12:15] Maya: on security docs, Olga needs SOC2 and encryption at rest details.
[12:19] Carlos: yes we'll share our SOC2 summary and KMS integration notes; Priya will include recommended caching patterns that preserve key secrecy.
[12:28] Ben: curious — any quick wins we can deploy in next 48 hours?
[12:31] Priya: yes — 1) reduce stream chunk size for chat to 32 tokens, 2) enable progressive flush for long completions, 3) increase ephemeral NAT pool on your side; bench these and report.
[12:42] Jordan: we'll try the chunk size change first.
[12:45] Carlos: great. to recap, we'll send: bench harness + configs (Priya), SOC2/KMS doc (Carlos), and a proposed pilot schedule. agreed next sync in one week after initial bench.
[12:58] Maya: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[13:02] Olga: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
